list.listitem: When clinically suspected, perform a complete eye exam with attention to slit-lamp and dilated fundus examination; refer to retinal specialist for optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiography. C
Consider systemic workup for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, arteriosclerosis; consider hypercoagulability or infectious/inflammatory workup in younger patients. C

Treatment is recommended for vision-threatening complications includes intravitreal anti-VEGF, corticosteroids, or focal laser for macular edema, panretinal photocoagulation for neovascularization, and vitrectomy for vitreous hemorrhage. A

background.definition: Blockage of blood flow within a branch retinal vein (BRVO) or the central retinal vein (CRVO). Although they are often grouped together, the natural history, risks of macular edema and neovascularization, treatments, and visual prognosis vary tremendously for BRVO and CRVO. B

list.listitem: BRVO: 5-year incidence 0.6%.
CRVO: 5-year incidence of 0.2%.
BRVO: prevalence of 0.6%.
CRVO: prevalence of 0.1%.
Retinal vein occlusions are the 2nd most common retinal vascular disorders after diabetic retinopathy.
Typically occur in patients older than 65, with incidence rate more than doubling every 10 years from second to seventh decade of life, but can occur at any age.
No hereditary pattern or gender predilection.
Black race associated with a higher risk of CRVO.
Hypertension.
Arteriosclerosis.
Diabetes mellitus, particularly those with end-organ damage.
Glaucoma, ocular hypertension.
Inflammatory or infectious (eg, sarcoidosis, SLE, syphilis, and Lyme disease).
Hyperviscosity (eg, polycythemia, leukemia, Waldenström's, and multiple myeloma).
Hypercoagulability (eg, lupus anticoagulant, protein C, S, or antithrombin III deficiency, hyperhomocysteinemia).
Optic disc drusen or edema (CRVO only).
Drugs (oral contraceptives, diuretics, and cocaine use).

In a systematic review of 21 studies of retinal vein occlusion, the percentage of cases attributed to hypertension was 47.9% (95% CI, 31.2%-63.1%), to hyperlipidemia 20.1% (95% CI, 5.9%-43.8%) and to diabetes mellitus 4.9% (95% CI, 0.8%-11.5%).

BRVO: arterial compression of vein within common adventitial sheath leads to turbulence, which combined with preexisting endothelial vascular damage promotes thrombus formation. Two-thirds of BRVO occur in the superotemporal quadrant.
CRVO: central retinal vein compressed by central retinal artery in area of lamina cribrosa, inducing thrombosis and causing resistance to venous blood flow.
Perform a full ocular examination with careful attention to presence of macular edema or ocular neovascularization. C
Consider systemic workup for hypertension, arteriosclerosis, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and other etiologies. C
Consider hypercoagulability workup in younger patients (<50 years). C
Obtain optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiogram by retinal specialist. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Typically bilateral, hemorrhages and microaneurysms concentrated in posterior pole, more prominent exudate
Narrowed retinal arterioles, hemorrhage throughout fundus, usually bilateral findings
Irregular and dilated (but not tortuous) veins, retinal hemorrhage in mid-periphery, disc neovascularization in 1/3, usually unilateral
History of radiation, more prominent cotton-wool spots, may have disc swelling, retinal neovascularization
Bilateral disc swelling and flame-shaped hemorrhage secondary to increased intracranial pressure

list.listitem: Vision loss with RVO is painless and unilateral but variable in presentation. It can be asymptomatic, can present with a blind spot or scotoma, or with sectoral or generalized vision loss (usually CRVO presents with worse vision). BRVO: superficial hemorrhage in a sector of the retina (limited to 1 side of the horizontal raphe) accompanied by a dilated and tortuous retinal vein. CRVO: diffuse retinal hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants with dilated and tortuous retinal veins, optic nerve edema, "blood and thunder" fundus.
Other signs seen in either: cotton wool spots, retinal edema, neovascularization of the iris, disc, or retina, vitreous hemorrhage.
No routine tests except blood pressure are indicated for diagnosis.

Retina specialist will perform optical coherence tomography to quantify macular edema and response to treatment, while fluorescein angiogram (FA) will diagnose retinal capillary nonperfusion, vascular remodeling, macular edema, and neovascularization.
Routine thrombophilia screen is not recommended.

Patient with decreased visual acuity must have complete ocular exam, including best-corrected visual acuity, pupillary reaction, intraocular pressure, confrontational fields, and slit-lamp exam. Gonioscopy can detect angle neovascularization in high-risk patients with significant retinal ischemia.
Most important is a dilated fundus examination to look for hemorrhage, macular edema, and neovascularization.

For CRVO, categorization into nonischemic and ischemic types is based on vision at presentation, presence of afferent pupillary defect, extent of hemorrhage, and capillary nonperfusion, and helps with assessment of prognosis and outcome.

Anti-VEGF treatments demonstrate clinically significant visual gains and are considered first-line therapy in the treatment for macular edema. Intravitreal corticosteroids are also effective and can be used in select cases. A
Grid/focal laser treatment is no longer considered first-line treatment but can be used as adjuvant therapy. A
For BRVO or CRVO, panretinal photocoagulation treatment may be necessary if ocular neovascularization develops. A
Treat any underlying medical conditions. Discontinue oral contraceptives if they are thought to be contributing to pathology.

Systemic medical treatment (ie, hemodilution, ticlopidine, troxerutin) for treatment of retinal vein occlusion is not recommended. Some ophthalmologists may recommend prophylactic aspirin, although no clinical trials demonstrate efficacy.

The mainstay for treatment for macular edema is intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept) treatment. Recent major randomized, controlled clinical trials (BRAVO/CRUISE/HORIZON/RETAIN for ranibizumab and COPERNICUS/GALILEO/VIBRANT for aflibercept) have demonstrated clinically significant improvements in visual acuity within several months of initiating monthly therapy, with sustained long-term effects on maintenance therapy. Earlier interventions lead to superior vision gains, and recommended therapy guidelines typically involve at least 3-6 months of fixed monthly dosing followed by a "treat and extend" or PRN regimen.
It may be worthwhle to monitor intraocular pressure after anti-VEGF treatment for up to 60 months after treatment.

Intravitreal corticosteroids (triamcinolone, dexamethasone) have also shown to improve visual acuity and reduce central retinal thickness in macular edema, demonstrated by recent major trials GENEVA, SCORE, and SOLO. Their duration of action may be longer and can decrease the treatment burden; they can be considered in patients with an incomplete response to anti-VEGF treatment, but patient selection is crucial, as steroid use can lead to higher risks of cataracts and glaucoma.

Individualized treatment regimens can optimize patient outcomes and minimize treatment burden. Intravitreal injection therapy can require long-term treatment to maintain initial vision gains, and must be balanced against risks which include pain, inflammation, infection, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal tear/detachment. Incidence of serious adverse effects are rare.
BRVO: Intravitreal injections have replaced grid/focal laser as the mainstay of treatment for macular edema.A
CRVO: Intravitreal injections are the mainstay of treatment for macular edema.A
Scatter (for BRVO) or panretinal (for CRVO) photocoagulation for iris, disc, or retinal neovascularization; prophylactic scatter laser is not indicated.
Vitrectomy for chronic macular edema refractory to other medical treatment can be considered but routine use is not recommended.
Vitrectomy for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage.
Other surgical treatments not proven (sheathotomy, radial optic neurotomy, choroidal-retinal anastomosis via laser or surgery).
Risk of BRVO and CRVO decreases with increasing levels of physical activity and alcohol consumption.
In women, risk decreases with use of postmenopausal estrogens.
Patients should be managed by a retinal specialist, with close follow-up every 1 to 2 months for initial 6 months to check for macular edema and neovascularization.
Follow-up individualized based on patient's response to treatment.
Vitreous hemorrhage, macular pucker, and other complications such as tractional or rhegmatogenous retinal detachments are treated with vitrectomy with or without scleral buckle.
Visual acuity at presentation is an important prognostic indicator of final visual outcome and risk of developing ocular neovascularization for CRVO and BRVO. A

The majority of patients with initially good vision (>20/40) maintain that vision, intermediate initial vision (20/50-20/200) has variable outcome, poor initial vision (<20/200) usually results in poor outcome. A
Intravitreal injections are capable of improving macular edema significantly in both BRVO and CRVO.

There are conflicting reports about association between retinal vein occlusion and mortality from cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events. Recent data suggests an overall increase in mortality in those with CRVO. B
RVO patients, especially male smokers, have an increased 10-year risk for cardiovascular disease.A
Avoid fluorescein angiogram during pregnancy or nursing.
